lines.text: Imagine starting a company to sell spices... and ending up powerful enough to rule millions of people.
That sounds impossible.
It does. But it actually happened. And it all started with a piece of paper.
It's always a piece of paper.
I'm Penny, this is Tiny Empires, and this is how a trading company took over India.
London. The last day of the year sixteen hundred. Queen Elizabeth the First grants a royal charter to a new company of merchants.
The Governor and Company of Merchants of London, trading into the East Indies. Thirty-first of December, sixteen hundred. Everyone just called it the East India Company.
The charter gave them a monopoly. No other English merchant could trade east of the Cape of Good Hope.
A monopoly means no competition. My favourite kind of market.
Investors put their money into the voyages. If the ships came home full, everyone got rich. If the ships sank...
Everyone got wet.
The prize was spice. Pepper, cloves and nutmeg were worth a fortune in Europe.
And the route was brutal. South past Africa, around the Cape of Good Hope, then across the Indian Ocean. Months at sea, each way.
The first fleet sailed in sixteen-oh-one under James Lancaster, and came home two years later, loaded with pepper.
Profit!
But there was a problem. The Dutch. Their own East India Company, founded in sixteen-oh-two, was bigger, richer, and very good at pushing rivals out of the Spice Islands.
In sixteen twenty-three, at Amboyna, the Dutch executed ten English traders. After that, the English largely turned away from the islands... and towards India.
Much of India was ruled by the Mughal Empire, one of the richest and most powerful states in the world. The Company did not arrive as a conqueror. It arrived asking for permission.
In sixteen-thirteen, under the emperor Jahangir, the English were allowed to open a trading post at Surat, on India's west coast.
Then an ambassador, Sir Thomas Roe, spent years at the Mughal court, asking for better terms.

Slowly, the trading posts multiplied. Madras, in sixteen thirty-nine. Bombay, which came to the English Crown as part of a royal wedding, and was handed to the Company in sixteen sixty-eight. And Calcutta, in Bengal, in sixteen-ninety.
And the big money moved from spice to cloth. Indian cotton and silk became hugely popular in Britain.
So what did the Company actually buy in India?
Cloth, mostly. Light, bright, washable cotton. Calico, named after Calicut. Painted chintz. And Bengal muslin, so fine it was called woven air.
By around seventeen hundred, cotton and silk cloth made up most of what the Company shipped home. Britain went wild for it.
So the empire started with... fashion?
Partly! English wool and silk weavers rioted in the streets, and Parliament banned wearing most printed cotton cloth, in seventeen twenty-one.
The Company also bought indigo for dye, saltpetre for gunpowder... and later, tea from China.
And it was run by young clerks called writers. Robert Clive arrived in Madras as an eighteen-year-old writer, copying letters and counting bales.
From office junior... to running a country. Okay, that's a career.
To protect their warehouses, the Company built forts... and hired soldiers. Many of them Indian sepoys.
Wait. A shop... with an army?
A shop with an army.
After the emperor Aurangzeb died in seventeen-oh-seven, Mughal power weakened, and regional rulers grew stronger. One of the richest regions was Bengal, ruled by a Nawab.
In seventeen fifty-six, a young new Nawab took over. Siraj ud-Daulah.
Siraj was furious. The Company was strengthening the defences of Calcutta without his permission, and abusing its trading privileges.
In June seventeen fifty-six, he marched on Calcutta and captured it.
So... the shop lost?
For now.
The Company sent soldiers from Madras, led by Robert Clive, along with a fleet under Admiral Charles Watson. Clive had started out in India as a clerk, and turned himself into a soldier.
On the second of January, seventeen fifty-seven, Clive and Admiral Watson took Calcutta back.
But Clive wanted more than Calcutta. Powerful people in Bengal were unhappy with Siraj. One of his own top army commanders, Mir Jafar. And the wealthy Jagat Seth bankers.
So a deal was made. Help us defeat the Nawab... and you become the new Nawab.
In return, Mir Jafar promised huge payments to the Company and its officers. The agreement was signed in secret, in June seventeen fifty-seven.
Is it normal to plan the result of a battle... before the battle?
It is when you've already bought the result.
Twenty-third of June, seventeen fifty-seven. Plassey. A mango grove beside the river.
Clive had about three thousand men, most of them Indian sepoys. The Nawab's army is usually put at around fifty thousand.
Then the monsoon rain arrived. Clive's gunners covered their powder with tarpaulins. Many of the Nawab's guns fell silent.
Keep your powder dry. Finally, advice I can follow.
And Mir Jafar? He kept his troops out of the fight.
The battle was over by the end of the day. Siraj fled, but he was captured and killed days later.
Mir Jafar became Nawab. But everyone knew who was really in charge.
The Company. Now it was collecting money, choosing rulers, and running an army.
When a later Nawab, Mir Qasim, tried to break free, war followed. In seventeen sixty-four, at Buxar, the Company defeated the combined armies of Mir Qasim, the ruler of Awadh, and the Mughal emperor.
And in seventeen sixty-five, the emperor Shah Alam the Second granted the Company the diwani. The right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
A company... collecting a country's taxes.
The traders had become rulers.
But remember. Plassey won Bengal, not India. It took many more decades of wars and treaties before the Company controlled most of the subcontinent.
In eighteen fifty-eight, after a great uprising, the British government took power away from the Company itself. And in eighteen seventy-four, the Company was dissolved.
From spices... to an empire... to closing down.
Not bad for a shop. Next time on Tiny Empires, we go back to the very beginning... to the lost cities of the Indus Valley, whose writing no one can read.
